findings.headline: Business rates collection 2.42% behind target, and declining 2.41% year-on-year
findings.detail: Business rates collection in Q1 is 2.42% behind the 27.70% target (£4.994m shortfall). The council attributes this partly to 'delays on the billing process due to government legislation changes' which should recover later in the year. However, collection is also 2.41% below the same period last year, suggesting underlying collection risk beyond timing.
findings.matters: Year-on-year business rates collection decline, beyond government billing delays, signals underlying income risk affecting cash flow and medium-term revenue.
findings.figures: £4.994m behind target (2.42%); 25.28% actual vs 27.70% target; down 2.41% year-on-year
findings.quote: Business rates collection is 2.42% behind target which equates to £4.994m. The figure of 25.28% is 2.41% below the previous year.

findings.headline: £51.3m of capital schemes decommissioned including 57 Greenford Rd housing block (£32.8m) cancelled
findings.detail: The council is removing £51.287m from the capital programme. The 57 Greenford Rd housing block purchase (£32.833m) is cancelled because 'the developer has withdrawn the offer to the council'. Stanhope Primary School development (£17.942m) is also decommissioned as the land sale capital receipt did not materialise. These cancellations substantially reduce housing investment delivery.
findings.matters: Capital cancellations of this scale reduce investment capacity; loss of £32.8m housing investment matters given the paper's identification of temporary accommodation cost pressures.
findings.figures: £51.287m total decommissioned; £32.833m (57 Greenford Rd housing); £17.942m (Stanhope Primary)
findings.quote: the purchase of the 57 Greenford Rd housing block that will no longer go ahead as the developer has withdrawn the offer to the council (£32.833m)

findings.headline: DSG deficit forecast to grow to £34.6m by year-end, driven by rising EHCP placement demand
findings.detail: The opening DSG deficit was £18.121m. In-year movements of £16.498m will push the closing balance to £34.619m. This is driven by increasing demand for Education, Health and Care Plan (EHCP) payments across mainstream, academy and independent schools. While government has signalled a High Needs Stability Grant covering 90% of the historic deficit, the ongoing annual deterioration continues.
findings.matters: DSG deficit is a balance sheet liability even if ring-fenced; structural EHCP demand growth represents ongoing recurring pressure that affects financial ratios.
findings.figures: Opening balance £18.121m; annual deterioration £16.498m; projected closing £34.619m
findings.quote: the forecast is estimating a deficit on DSG of £16.498m, which is due to an increase in the High Needs Block across several areas relating to Education Health and Care Plan (EHCP) payments to schools

findings.headline: Only 30% of £11.9m approved savings achieved by Q1; £2.6m at risk of not delivering
findings.detail: The council approved £11.937m of net savings for 2026/27. At Q1, only £3.604m (30.19%) have been achieved, with £2.595m (21.74%) flagged as at risk. Children's Services is particularly weak at 22.82% achievement with £1.495m red-rated.
findings.matters: Weak savings delivery early in the year signals the council will need alternative budget actions, indicating execution and financial resilience risk.
findings.figures: £3.604m achieved (30.19%); £2.595m at risk (21.74%); £5.738m in progress
findings.quote: At the end of Q1, £3.604m (30.19%) of the savings have been achieved with £2.595m (21.74%) identified at being risk

findings.headline: Adult social care placement costs driving two-thirds of service overspend, a structural demand pressure
findings.detail: Adult Services & Public Health is forecasting £12.459m overspend, of which £12.849m is attributed to long-term placements for learning disability, mental health and older adults. The paper identifies 'high-cost clients' as a key risk, indicating this pressure is expected to persist.
findings.matters: Demand-led social care pressures that exceed budgets represent recurring, uncontrollable costs that affect financial sustainability and credit risk.
findings.figures: £12.459m Adult Services overspend; £12.849m from long-term placements
findings.quote: £12.849m pressure relating to the cost of long-term learning disability, mental health & older adults placements.

findings.headline: £7.8m General Fund overspend in Q1 being masked by contingency use, which the council explicitly states is unsustainable
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a net overspend of £7.797m (1.84%) at Q1, comprised of £19.879m service overspends offset by £12.082m corporate underspends (including £5.0m contingency use and £1.0m treasury management gains). The council states: 'it is crucial that every possible action is taken to reduce non-essential expenditure at this early stage of the financial year to deliver a balanced budget'.
findings.matters: Lenders need to know whether overspends are real structural problems or accounting moves; early-year reliance on contingencies signals the former.
findings.figures: £7.797m net overspend; £19.879m service overspends offset by £12.082m corporate underspends including £5.0m contingency
findings.quote: Given the level of contingencies that are assumed within the forecast position, it is crucial that every possible action is taken to reduce non-essential expenditure at this early stage of the financial year to deliver a balanced budget by the end of financial year

findings.headline: Children's Social Care is underspending but requires £4.2m of mitigation actions to stay on track
findings.detail: Children's Social Care shows an underspend of £1.8m but requires £4.2m of mitigation actions, partially offset by £344k of negative mitigation. This pattern suggests the service is being actively suppressed below baseline to achieve an underspend, rather than naturally spending less.
findings.matters: A service that requires substantial mitigation to underspend suggests underlying cost pressures. If mitigations are not sustained or become unsustainable, this could flip to significant overspend.
findings.figures: Budget £54,028k, requires mitigation £4,200k, underspend shown £(1,820)k
findings.quote: Children´s Social Care 1BB Children´s Social Care 54,028 0 54,028 13,510 48,352 0 0 4,200 (344) 0 0 0 52,208 (1,820)

findings.headline: Housing Demand is overrunning by £3.6m despite £6.9m of management actions being deployed
findings.detail: Housing Demand (predominantly temporary accommodation and housing support) is budgeted at £28.8m but forecast to outturn at £32.4m. Management actions of £6.9m have been applied but the service is still £3.6m over. This suggests demand is outpacing both budget and management interventions.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation and housing support costs are often volatile and demand-driven. An overspend that persists despite active management suggests either policy changes driving demand or a structural gap between budget and need.
findings.figures: Budget £28,772k, forecast £32,380k, overspend £3,608k despite management actions of £6,877k

findings.headline: The entire £5m contingency budget has been allocated by Q1
findings.detail: Contingency was budgeted at £5.0m but is forecast to be fully deployed with zero forecast variance. This means the council has no emergency buffer remaining for the nine months from October onwards.
findings.matters: Depleting the entire contingency reserve by October leaves the council with no emergency buffer for unexpected costs or demand spikes for the remainder of the financial year.
findings.figures: Contingency budget £5,000k, forecast £0k, variance (£5,000)k
findings.quote: Contingency 1CB Centrally Held Contingency 5,000 0 5,000 0 0 0 0 (5,000)

findings.headline: £5.5m of efficiency savings remain unallocated at Q1 and will be vired to services in Q2
findings.detail: The annual budget assumes £5.5m of efficiency savings, but these have not yet been identified or assigned to services. The council notes these will be vired in Q2 and 'service forecasts updated in Q2'. This means the full-year delivery of the savings plan is not yet confirmed.
findings.matters: If efficiency savings of this magnitude are not achieved, they flow directly into the forecast variance. A council unable to identify savings this late in Q1 faces execution risk for the full year.
findings.figures: £5,527k efficiency savings shown as 'will be vired to services in Q2'
findings.quote: Efficiency saving budgets are shown within the net cost of services. This budget will be vired to services in Q2 and service forecasts updated in Q2 (5,527)

findings.headline: Adult social care is running £12.5m over budget (10.5% overspend) in the first quarter
findings.detail: Adult Services are forecast at £131.5m against a budget of £119.1m. Management actions of £620k have been applied but the service remains significantly overrun. This is demand-driven and suggests either demographic pressures or cost inflation in care provision. Social care is typically the largest pressure point for councils.
findings.matters: A 10% overspend in the largest revenue service within three months signals underlying cost inflation or demand growth that could persist across the financial year and reduce the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Budget £119,083k, forecast £131,542k, overspend £12,459k

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation acquisition (Phase 3) is slipped by £17.201m
findings.detail: Temporary accommodation acquisition schemes are showing significant slippage of £17.201m. This is material given Ealing's known pressures with temporary housing costs, which drive substantial revenue spending and were flagged in recent budget reports.
findings.matters: Delays in temporary accommodation capital schemes mean the council continues incurring higher revenue costs for temporary placements. This affects financial resilience if TA spending cannot be brought under control through capital delivery.
findings.figures: Temporary Accommodation Acquisition (Phase 3) slippage: £17.201m
findings.quote: GC4181 TEMPORARY ACCOMMODATION ACQUISITION (PHASE 3)

findings.headline: Ealing has £262.190m of capital slippage with zero acceleration offsetting it
findings.detail: The council has deferred £262.190m of planned capital spending across all service areas. The General Fund alone accounts for £130.388m of this, and there is no acceleration (acceleration column shows 0.000 across all lines), meaning no brought-forward spending from other periods is making up for the delays.
findings.matters: Capital slippage of this magnitude indicates delivery challenges across housing, schools, and corporate property schemes. For lenders, it raises questions about project management and the council's ability to execute its capital programme, particularly given housing pressures.
findings.figures: Total slippage: £262.190m; General Fund slippage: £130.388m; no acceleration: 0.000

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Statement of Accounts and AGS 2025-26
findings.headline: General Fund balance held at £21.3m (5.2% of net budget), progressively moving towards London borough average
findings.detail: The General Fund balance increased by £0.78m to £21.252m, bringing the council 'progressively in line with the general balances held by other London boroughs.' This is noted as meeting the sector guidance minimum of at least 5% of net budget requirement. The balance is adequate for statutory purposes but offers limited headroom for demand shocks.
findings.matters: A 5% reserve is statutory minimum; it is not a buffer. If a demand surge (homelessness, social care) occurs mid-year, the council has little discretionary cash to manage it without drawing on earmarked reserves or revising the budget in-year.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £21.252m; 2024-25 opening balance £19.402m, 2025-26 closing £21.252m (increase £1.850m including transfer); in-year movement £0.780m
findings.quote: This is in line with sector guidance that suggests that the general balance should be at least 5% of the net budget requirement and brings the council progressively in line with the general balances held by other London boroughs

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Statement of Accounts and AGS 2025-26
findings.headline: Performance indicators: 33% of available KPIs did not meet targets, signalling service strain
findings.detail: Of 60 available KPIs at Q2, 33% (20) were rated Red (below target), including fly-tip clearance, graffiti removal, adult social care satisfaction, EHC plans, school attainment for Black Caribbean pupils, and FOI response times. The council extended fly-tip response target from 24 hours to 48 hours due to demand. Adult social care satisfaction fell to 52.6% against a 60% target. These indicators suggest stretched capacity across multiple services.
findings.matters: Widespread KPI misses, even if individually explainable, suggest the council is stretched. Demand is outpacing service capacity in multiple areas, not just social care. This compounds budget risk: if performance pressures mount, the cost of remedial action rises.
findings.figures: Q2 2025-26: 20 Red, 13 Amber, 27 Green, 14 N/A out of 74 indicators (33% did not meet target)
findings.quote: Of the 60 indicators available at the reporting date 33% did not meet their target, while 67% had either met their target or were within tolerance

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Statement of Accounts and AGS 2025-26
findings.headline: Medium-term funding forecast shows a £7.9m gap opening in 2028-29
findings.detail: The MTFS table shows total expenditure growing to £505.389m by 2028-29 while funding is projected at £497.496m, creating an unallocated shortfall of £7.893m. This assumes savings plans are delivered as shown, the LGFS remains as currently forecast, and Business Rates reset proceeds as planned. No savings have yet been identified to close this gap.
findings.matters: A funding gap three years out, even if notional, signals that the council does not yet have a pathway to balance. If any of the assumptions slip (grant reductions, higher demand, savings shortfall), the gap widens immediately.
findings.figures: 2028-29 funding gap: £7.893m (expenditure £505.389m, funding £497.496m)

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Statement of Accounts and AGS 2025-26
findings.headline: Medium-term savings plan of £20.5m becomes progressively harder to deliver without affecting front-line services
findings.detail: The MTFS identifies savings of £11.937m for 2026-27, declining to £1.279m by 2029-30 (total £20.476m). The narrative states: 'Continuing to identify and deliver significant savings plans has become increasingly challenging without affecting front-line services for residents.' Children's Services alone faces £13.539m cumulative savings over the MTFS period. The council is pursuing new operating models and transformation, but the savings trajectory is steep relative to demand growth.
findings.matters: A savings plan that the council itself describes as 'increasingly challenging' suggests that further rounds are likely to be difficult. If demand pressures continue and savings fall short, the council will face budget pressure in 2027-28 onwards.
findings.quote: Continuing to identify and deliver significant savings plans has become increasingly challenging without affecting front-line services for residents

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Statement of Accounts and AGS 2025-26
findings.headline: Working-age admissions to permanent residential care rising faster than target
findings.detail: As of Q2 2025-26, there were 17 admissions to permanent residential and nursing care for working-age adults (18-64), slightly above the target of 14 (rate 6.7 per 100,000 vs target 6.1). The narrative notes that 'placement activity for working age adults has been noted as an area of growing demand and cost' and that 'admissions to residential and nursing care homes for service users [are] rising across England.' The council has complex cases under review through a transformation programme and strengthened review panels, but the trend is upward.
findings.matters: Working-age admissions to residential care are expensive, typically £30–50k per person per year, and indicate either population health decline, insufficient community support, or complex cases unable to be managed at home. Rising admissions are a cost and demand forecast risk.
findings.figures: 17 admissions (target 14); rate 6.7 per 100,000 (target 6.1)
findings.quote: Placement activity for working age adults has been noted as an area of growing demand and cost, with admissions to residential and nursing care homes for service users rising across England

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Statement of Accounts and AGS 2025-26
findings.headline: Education, Health and Care plan backlog: only 43% issued within 20 weeks against 46% target
findings.detail: Demand for EHC plan assessments continues to rise in line with regional and national trends. The council faces backlog pressures, national shortages of educational psychologists, and delays from NHS partners in providing health information. Despite targeted investment, Q2 performance of 43% (up from 32% in Q1) remains below the 46% target. The council aims to reach the target by year-end but the service is under sustained pressure.
findings.matters: EHC plan delays mean children do not access funded provision when assessed as needing it, creating legal exposure and parental dissatisfaction. This is a statutory duty under the Children and Families Act 2014, and delays signal capacity constraint in the SEN system.
findings.figures: Q2 2025-26: 43% of EHC plans issued within 20 weeks (Q1: 32%, target: 46%)
findings.quote: Demand in relation to Education, Health and Care (EHC) plan needs assessments continues to rise in line with regional and national trends, leading to backlog pressures across the service

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Statement of Accounts and AGS 2025-26
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation demand has risen substantially and is now straining the general fund
findings.detail: The narrative identifies a 'substantial rise in the need for temporary accommodation' as adding strain to the general fund. This reflects the homelessness approaches documented in performance metrics and aligns with the London-wide trend. The council is using HRA properties to house temporary accommodation tenants (yielding additional income this year), but this is a one-off benefit, not a structural solution to rising homelessness.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is expensive, demand-led, and difficult to reduce once in place. Rising homelessness in a wealthy London borough signals both housing shortage and poverty in the resident base, and pressures the general fund annually.
findings.figures: No specific figure given; HRA achieved additional income from 'letting regeneration void properties for temporary accommodation tenants' as a favourable variance
findings.quote: substantial rise in the need for temporary accommodation adding further strain to the general fund

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Statement of Accounts and AGS 2025-26
findings.headline: Service overspends of £13.5m exceeded what corporate budgets could cover, eating into reserves
findings.detail: Adults and Public Health overspent by £9.027m, Children's and Schools by £6.968m, totalling £13.5m in service-level overspends. The council had budgeted for growth in these areas, but actual demand and market conditions surpassed expectations. Corporate budgets saved £13.684m, mostly from interest on cash balances, leaving only a £0.78m underspend transferred to reserves. This means demand-led spending is outrunning both growth allocations and corporate contingencies.
findings.matters: When services overspend by this scale and are only absorbed by non-structural corporate income (interest on balances), the underlying budget is not sustainable. Interest rates will not always be high, and the demand will continue.
findings.figures: Services overspent £13.538m; Adults overspend £9.027m; Children's overspend £6.968m; underspend transferred to reserves £0.780m
findings.quote: actual demand and market conditions have surpassed expectations, resulting in overspending in demand-led services such as social care, homelessness, and temporary accommodation

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Draft Statement of Accounts and AGS 2025-26
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit now £18.5m and driven entirely by High Needs pressure
findings.detail: The DSG account closed with a net deficit of £18.519m (updated to £18.121m after final adjustments), comprising a High Needs block deficit of £18.366m and a Schools Block deficit of £0.153m. This is a ring-fenced account that cannot draw on the General Fund. The High Needs deficit grew by £12.878m in-year alone and reflects structural pressure in the service from demand rising faster than funding allows.
findings.matters: A growing DSG deficit signals that the council is unable to fund statutory special educational needs and alternative provision within settlement limits, and must carry the growing liability forward year on year. This is a risk marker for councils facing unsustainable demand for high-cost placements.
findings.figures: £18.519m net DSG deficit (opening £5.641m, in-year movement £12.878m); High Needs block £18.366m deficit
findings.quote: net deficit balance of £18.519m on its DSG account which includes a High Needs DSG deficit of £18.366m

findings.paper_title: Annual Conclusion and Quarter 4 Internal Audit and Investigation Update Report
findings.headline: Building Safety Act compliance has multiple unresolved issues with unclear timelines
findings.detail: Three building safety audit findings remain outstanding: tracking and reporting progress (status 'Partially Implemented'), building safety cases not current for High Rise Buildings (status 'TBC' with audit awaiting evidence), and lack of golden thread system in place (status unclear). Original deadlines were April 2026 and have been extended to TBC (to be confirmed), with no revised dates provided.
findings.matters: Building Safety Act compliance is statutory. Unresolved issues with unclear implementation dates represent legal and reputational risk, and the 'TBC' status suggests remediation planning is incomplete.
findings.figures: 3 Building Safety Act findings; original deadline April 2026 now TBC with no revised date confirmed
findings.quote: Building Safety Act – Housing – Follow up work: Building Safety Cases not current for all HRBs. Initially April 2026 now tbc. Management have advised completed, but internal audit are awaiting submission of evidence to support.

findings.paper_title: Annual Conclusion and Quarter 4 Internal Audit and Investigation Update Report
findings.headline: Control opinion was already at risk last year and has not materially improved
findings.detail: The CAE's conclusion is that controls are effective, but the historical comparison is telling: 2024/25 opinion was Reasonable 'but on the cusp of limited due to the number of lower assurance reports.' This year still has 2 limited assurance reports (housing complaints, repairs and adaptations, corporate property) and the opinion remains Reasonable, suggesting the control environment has not strengthened.
findings.matters: A control environment that was at the borderline of 'Limited' assurance last year and has not materially improved in the subsequent year suggests systemic issues are not being resolved.
findings.figures: 2024/25: Reasonable opinion 'on the cusp of limited'; 2025/26: Reasonable with 2 Limited assurance reports (originally 3, one resolved)
findings.quote: For information, this compares with 2024/25 where the overall opinion was Reasonable but on the cusp of limited due to the number of lower assurance reports.

findings.paper_title: Annual Conclusion and Quarter 4 Internal Audit and Investigation Update Report
findings.headline: Housing voids backlog remains above target with implementation date now extended to March 2027
findings.detail: The voids follow-up audit identified delays in pre and post-inspection completion of key fields. The original implementation date was May 2024, extended to July 2026, with the backlog issue itself now not expected to be resolved until March 2027. The paper notes voids turnaround has improved but 'remains above the target.'
findings.matters: Housing voids represent both capital asset utilization and rental income loss. A backlog extending to 2027 indicates operational/management control issues affecting a material revenue stream for a council with significant housing stock.
findings.figures: Original deadline May 2024 → July 2026 → March 2027 for voids backlog resolution
findings.quote: Voids turn around has been improved, but remains above the target.

findings.paper_title: Annual Conclusion and Quarter 4 Internal Audit and Investigation Update Report
findings.headline: 14 high-risk audit recommendations remain outstanding with repeated implementation date slippages
findings.detail: The council has 14 high-risk audit findings awaiting remediation, up from 6 in Q3. Multiple items have missed original deadlines and been pushed back repeatedly: voids backlog now extended to March 2027 (originally January 2025), data protection reporting now January 2027 (originally November 2025), building safety cases status unclear (originally April 2026). Several actions management claimed completed have been found by audit testing to still be in progress.
findings.matters: Outstanding high-risk audit findings indicate control weaknesses are not being fixed promptly, suggesting management capacity or priority issues. Repeated date slippages raise questions about the council's ability to execute remediation plans.
findings.figures: 14 high-risk recommendations outstanding (up from 6 in Q3); multiple remediation dates pushed back 6-14 months
findings.quote: There are 14 high risk recommendations that remain outstanding, which compares to 6 in quarter 3.

findings.headline: Social care and construction market failures narrowing supplier options and increasing costs
findings.detail: The Supplier/Market Failure risk (unmitigated score 24, mitigated 16) explicitly cites 'Recent examples of failure of construction firms, pressures and rising costs in social care market (adults and children's), private landlords leaving the market for temporary accommodation, limited market for repairs and maintenance contractors' alongside ongoing construction downturn limiting estate regeneration options.
findings.matters: Market tightness for social care suppliers and construction firms constrains the council's options and increases emergency repair/care costs; supplier failure examples suggest capacity is genuinely limited, not just pricing.
findings.figures: Supplier/Market Failure risk score: 24 unmitigated, 16 mitigated
findings.quote: Recent examples of failure of construction firms, pressures and rising costs in social care market (adults and children's), private landlords leaving the market for temporary accommodation, limited market for repairs and maintenance contractors and with the ongoing downturn in the construction industry limited market for estate regeneration projects.

findings.headline: Council taking direct operational control of stalled development sites previously managed through council-owned vehicles
findings.detail: The council states 'Work on the stalled BL / BLRP sites now been reviewed and will be led by the Council,' appearing under the Supplier/Market Failure risk. This indicates council-owned development vehicles have stalled projects that the council is reassuming control of, suggesting those vehicles were unable to deliver.
findings.matters: Stalled development projects represent capital tied up with uncertain return; the transfer from arm's-length vehicles to direct council management signals those vehicles underperformed and the council must absorb delivery risk.
findings.figures: Number and value of sites not disclosed
findings.quote: Work on the stalled BL / BLRP sites now been reviewed and will be led by the Council.

findings.headline: Homelessness temporary accommodation costs forcing service redesign ahead of 2026/27
findings.detail: The council identifies 'Cost pressures with the homelessness service (TA)' as part of the Financial Resilience risk, with planned 'Review of programme and priorities ahead of 2026/27' that implies service reductions or refocusing. The mitigation strategy includes 'Housing Demand Programme to mitigation financial pressures,' suggesting anticipated budget constraints are driving operational change.
findings.matters: Homelessness TA is often the fastest-growing and least controllable spend; planned service model changes indicate the council expects to constrain this budget through redesign rather than volume reductions.
findings.figures: Not quantified; described as significant cost pressure driving 2026/27 programme review
findings.quote: Cost pressures with the homelessness service (TA). Review of programme and priorities ahead of 2026/27– to refocus effort and resources.

findings.headline: Council's capital financing requirement of £1,043m exceeds external borrowing by £201m, with the gap covered by internal borrowing.
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement stands at £1,043.462m against actual borrowing of £841.973m. The council explicitly confirms: "borrowing requirements are financed through both external and internal borrowing, although no external borrowing was raised during the financial year". This £201.489m gap is being filled through reserves.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing (cash use) is a finite strategy; as reserves deplete, the council will need to raise external borrowing, potentially at rates higher than locked-in borrowing costs.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement £1,043.462m, external borrowing £841.973m, creating a £201.489m internal borrowing gap
findings.quote: The council's actual borrowing stood at £841.973m which is below the CFR of £1,043.462m. The council's borrowing requirements are financed through both external and internal borrowing, although no external borrowing was raised during the financial year.

findings.headline: Investment balances fell 30% as council funded capital expenditure from cash reserves rather than external borrowing.
findings.detail: Council investment balances declined from £417.056m to £290.109m (£126.947m decrease) over the year. The paper explicitly links this to capital funding: "cash balances are used to fund capital expenditure". This is a significant drawdown of the council's liquid reserves in a single year.
findings.matters: Cash reserves are finite; capital funded from reserves rather than sustainable borrowing will eventually deplete working capital or force external borrowing.
findings.figures: Investment balance £417.056m (31 March 2025) to £290.109m (31 March 2026), a decrease of £126.947m or 30.4%
findings.quote: There is a decrease in the investment balance from £417.056m at 31 March 2025 to £290.109m at 31 March 2026 as cash balances are used to fund capital expenditure.

findings.headline: Council tax and business rates collection both fell 1.12% short of target, leaving £4.999m uncollected in-year.
findings.detail: Council tax in-year collection was 95.88%, missing the 97% target by £2.933m. Business rates collection was 95.38%, missing the 96.5% target by £2.066m. Council tax collection deteriorated 0.97% against the prior year, suggesting collection pressure is worsening.
findings.matters: Collection shortfalls reduce in-year income and require management action or service cuts to stay in balance. Deteriorating collection is a leading indicator of resident and business financial stress within the district.
findings.figures: Council tax shortfall £2.933m (1.12% below 97% target). Business rates shortfall £2.066m (1.12% below 96.5% target). Combined £4.999m uncollected.
findings.quote: Council tax in-year collection was 95.88% which is 1.12% behind the target collection profile (97%) which equates to £2.933m.

findings.headline: Council is deliberately building general fund reserves to £21.252m (6.5% of budget) to manage financial uncertainty, while noting other London boroughs' balances are reducing.
findings.detail: The General Fund balance was increased by the 2025/26 underspend to £21.252m. The S151 Officer's March 2026 risk assessment set the adequate range at £17.5m–£25m. The paper notes the council is now 'increasing its balances at a time where other London boroughs' balances are reducing,' suggesting Ealing faces sharper financial stress than its peers.
findings.matters: A council building reserves while peers draw them down signals it expects sustained financial stress. The explicit comparison (other boroughs reducing balances) suggests Ealing's underlying pressures exceed the sector average.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £21.252m at 31 March 2026 (6.5% of net budget requirement). Opening balance £20.472m. S151 Officer adequate range £17.5m–£25m.
findings.quote: The council is increasing its balances at a time where other London boroughs' balances are reducing.

findings.headline: £18.366m High Needs Block DSG deficit persists despite statutory reforms; new stability grant covers only 90% of accumulated deficit.
findings.detail: The council reports a ring-fenced DSG deficit of £18.366m on the High Needs Block. The paper notes that 'Around 90% of High Need Block funding is committed to meeting statutory duties for pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), limiting flexibility to manage in-year pressures.' Although a new High Needs Stability Grant will fund 90% of the historic deficit from 2026/27, the paper warns that reform programmes 'will not address the current level of financial pressure in the short term.'
findings.matters: This is a ring-fenced deficit that cannot be subsidised from the General Fund. It must be cleared from DSG income. The partial grant leaves 10% of the historic deficit unfunded and does not resolve ongoing pressure.
findings.figures: DSG cumulative deficit £18.519m (High Needs £18.366m, Schools Block £0.153m). High Needs Stability Grant covers 90% of the High Needs deficit from 2026/27.
findings.quote: Around 90% of High Need Block funding is committed to meeting statutory duties for pupils with Education, Health and Care Plans (EHCPs), limiting flexibility to manage in-year pressures.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspend of £7.519m driven by housing benefit subsidy shortfall, a structural pressure reflecting national housing shortage.
findings.detail: Housing & Environment overspent by £7.519m on temporary accommodation, mainly due to 'housing benefit subsidy shortfall, other temporary accommodation net costs and an increase in the bad debt provision.' This is a demand-driven pressure reflecting the national shortage of permanent housing stock and reflects policy constraints (council cannot refuse homeless duties).
findings.matters: This is a structural pressure Ealing cannot control, rooted in national housing policy and shortage. It will persist and likely grow, representing a fixed cost drain on the budget.
findings.figures: Temporary accommodation overspend £7.519m within £1.993m Housing & Environment underspend.
findings.quote: Temporary accommodation overspend of £7.519m mainly relates to housing benefit subsidy shortfall, other temporary accommodation net costs and an increase in the bad debt provision.

findings.headline: Paper warns explicitly that demand-led cost and volume pressures will persist into 2026/27 despite budget growth, signalling sustained financial stress ahead.
findings.detail: The outturn summary states that although an underspend was delivered, 'significant overspends were experienced, especially in demand led services. Whilst budget growth has been included in many of these budgets for 2026/27, there remain significant ongoing risks of rising costs, demand and complexity of that demand that will need to be managed to achieve a balanced outturn for 2026/27.' This is an explicit admission the structural problem will not be solved.
findings.matters: The council is signalling it expects 2026/27 to remain difficult. Growth already allocated may not be sufficient, suggesting a budget-setting challenge ahead and potential further deficits or reserve draws.
findings.figures: No 2026/27 figures provided; forward-looking warning only.
findings.quote: Whilst budget growth has been included in many of these budgets for 2026/27, there remain significant ongoing risks of rising costs, demand and complexity of that demand that will need to be managed to achieve a balanced outturn for 2026/27.

findings.headline: The council's £0.780m underspend is entirely dependent on one-off interest income and capital delays; remove these and the position is £5m overspent.
findings.detail: The reported underspend is 'principally due to the interest earned on cash balances... due to interest rates remaining higher for longer than anticipated and delays in the capital programme.' Quarter 3 forecast showed a £5.023m overspend before these temporary benefits. Services overspent by £13.540m but this was masked by £13.684m of corporate underspends (interest income). This is not sustainable.
findings.matters: The headline outturn is misleading. The actual service position is structurally overspent by £5m+. When interest rates normalise and capital catch-up spending occurs, the council's true financial position will be exposed.
findings.figures: Outturn underspend £0.780m. Services net overspend £13.540m. Corporate budget underspend £13.684m (interest-driven). Q3 forecast showed £5.023m overspend.
findings.quote: The additional interest, and other one-off or time-limited corporate budgets and contingencies, enabled the council to off-set service overspends and contribute to general balances by £0.780m (0.24% of the net revenue budget).

findings.headline: £9.027m overspend in adults social care and £6.968m in children's services despite budget growth, driven by placement cost inflation the council cannot control.
findings.detail: Adults & Public Health overspent by £9.027m, primarily due to placement pressures with a gross placements overspend of £17.106m. Children's & Schools overspent by £6.968m, with residential care alone costing £4.828m over budget. The paper notes average weekly cost increases of £2.9m in children's residential care since 2024/25, reflecting market-rate inflation rather than volume.
findings.matters: These are structural pressures driven by market costs and statutory duties, not controllable by the council. Even with allocated growth, costs are running ahead. This pattern is forecast to continue into 2026/27.
findings.figures: Adults overspend £9.027m. Children's overspend £6.968m. Placement gross overspend £17.106m. Children's residential care average weekly increase £2.9m since 2024/25.
findings.quote: Despite that growth, these severe pressures remain and have resulted in overspends across these areas.

findings.headline: Large ongoing capital programme funded substantially by borrowing: £321m new debt needed in 2026/27 alone
findings.detail: The council plans capital expenditure of £511m–£536m annually. After grants and reserves, this leaves a net financing need of £321.589m for 2026/27, requiring substantial new borrowing. The pace of capital spending and debt accumulation outpaces MRP paydown significantly.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess debt trajectory and whether the council's revenue income is sufficient to service accumulated debt. The CFR rises from £1,022m to £1,691m by 2028/29—a 65% increase—while investment balances are shrinking.
findings.figures: Total capital programme 2026/27: £511.566m; net financing need: £321.589m; CFR: 2024/25 £1,022m → 2028/29 £1,691m
findings.quote: Total Capital Programme ... 511.566 ... Net Financing Need (General Fund & HRA - Borrowing) ... 321.589

findings.headline: Council borrowed £869m early in 2021/22 at low rates; capital programme delayed, leaving overborrowed position
findings.detail: The council took advantage of low rates to borrow in advance of need in 2021/22, but the projects those loans were meant to fund have experienced delays due to COVID and economic factors. The council now carries debt it doesn't yet need to spend, raising refinancing and carry-cost questions.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the timing mismatch (debt drawn early, projects delayed) represents a prudent strategy or a bet on rates that backfired. If rates rise further, the carry cost is locked in; if the projects stall, liquidity is needlessly tied up.
findings.figures: Total external debt 31 March 2025: £861.894m; CFR: £1,022.394m (under-borrowed by £160.5m)
findings.quote: the council took advantage of low interest rates borrowings in 2021/22 to fund its planned capital programme. That capital programme has experienced delays due to the impact of covid and the wider economic position, however, the overborrowing position is expected to reduce over the next couple of years.

findings.headline: Policy investment in BLRP housing loans dominates future net financing, rising from 7% to 86% of borrowing need
findings.detail: Broadway Living Registered Provider (BLRP) loans represent a growing concentration of debt. In 2028/29 alone, borrowing for BLRP is £316.241m—86% of total new financing need—with a 50-year repayment schedule and a development-phase repayment holiday. This creates exposure to a single asset class and operator over multiple decades.
findings.matters: A lender assessing total debt needs to understand that a third of the council's 2028/29 debt is concentrated in a housing development entity. If BLRP falters, the council faces a material refinancing risk and credit loss exposure.
findings.figures: BLRP borrowing 2026/27: £57.647m (16.68% of net financing); 2028/29: £316.241m (86.21% of net financing)
findings.quote: Housing Loan to BLRP ... 57.647 ... 316.241 ... Percentage of total net financing need % ... 16.68% ... 86.21%

findings.headline: HRA unable to independently finance its borrowing need and relying on General Fund support
findings.detail: The Housing Revenue Account is not borrowing independently despite a significant capital programme, instead drawing on General Fund cash balances and temporary borrowing. The council is waiting for interest rates to fall before undertaking HRA borrowing—a form of rate speculation that creates dependency on the GF if rates don't fall as expected.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether HRA finances are stressed and whether GF support is sustainable. If rates don't fall, the HRA may face a funding crisis and draw down GF resources meant for other services.
findings.figures: HRA revenues 2026/27: £98.911m; HRA debt forecast to rise to £452.193m by 2026/27
findings.quote: Currently the interest rates are not favourable for new borrowings and interest rates are expected to fall in the coming years, at which point the council will consider undertaking HRA borrowing. In the meantime, it will utilise cash balances and, if necessary, borrow in the short term from the GF.

findings.headline: Cash reserves declining sharply from £527m to £175m over four years
findings.detail: The council's expected investment balances are forecast to fall by two-thirds over the planning period. By 2028/29, balances drop to just £175m—a liquidity position that narrows the council's buffer against cash flow volatility and reduces flexibility for responding to unexpected demands.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's cash headroom is shrinking, which could constrain flexibility to meet obligations or absorb shocks without additional borrowing at potentially unfavorable rates.

findings.headline: Business rates safety net falls from 100% to 92.5% after 2026/27, exposing council to collection shortfalls
findings.detail: Government protection on business rates falls from 100% safety net in 2026/27 to 97% in 2027/28 and 92.5% from 2028/29 onwards. The council's forecast collection of £236.277m is vulnerable to local economic conditions affecting business valuations and occupancy. Any shortfall below the declining safety net threshold directly reduces the council's available funding. The council acknowledges this risk 'will need to be closely monitored during the year.'
findings.matters: Business rates income is volatile. The declining government protection means economic downturns affecting the borough's business base will reduce council income without equivalent compensation, directly threatening financial sustainability in a weaker economy.
findings.figures: 100% safety net 2026/27, declining to 97% (2027/28) and 92.5% (2028/29); £236.277m total collection forecast, £70.883m retained by council, £0.238m safety net payment expected 2026/27
findings.quote: The Safety Net threshold will gradually revert to 92.5% for most authorities over the settlement period. Therefore, based on current estimates the council will expect to receive a safety net payment of £0.238m in 2026/27. This safety net payment will ensure the council received the government assumed business rates baseline in 2026/27, although there will be risks to the baseline income in future years should the council's business rates base reduce.

findings.headline: High Needs Block pressure forcing continued 0.5% transfer from mainstream schools funding
findings.detail: The council continues the 0.5% transfer from Schools Block to High Needs Block in 2026/27 (£1.712m) as a mitigation for SEND funding shortfall. The document states the council is 'currently faced with a projected pressure which is being partially mitigated through revised management actions'—the language 'currently' and 'partially' indicates the underlying pressure remains unresolved and is merely being managed through inter-block transfers that reduce mainstream schools' funding.
findings.matters: This reveals an ongoing structural mismatch between SEND demand and SEND funding that the council is managing through transfers from mainstream schools. If this pressure escalates or the transfer cannot continue, it creates risk to both SEND provision and schools' operational budgets.
findings.figures: 0.5% transfer (£1.712m) from Schools Block to High Needs Block in 2026/27, described as continuation of previous years' transfers
findings.quote: The council is currently faced with a projected pressure which is being partially mitigated through revised management actions, including the continued 0.5% transfer from the SB in 2026/27

findings.headline: £18.6m combined pressure in children's and adults' social care pressures continuing through 2029
findings.detail: Children's Services faces £12.796m pressure in 2026/27 (forecast £3.664m in 2027/28, £1.487m in 2028/29), and Adult Social Care £6.539m (forecast £4.549m in 2027/28, £3.649m in 2028/29). Temporary accommodation adds a further £5.824m pressure in 2026/27. The council notes these challenges are 'especially pronounced for the council as a London borough' due to housing costs and demographic factors. These are demand-driven pressures, not efficiency issues, and the council projects they will persist.
findings.matters: Structural demand pressures in statutory services (social care, homelessness) cannot be easily controlled through efficiency savings alone, creating ongoing budget risk and vulnerability to in-year overspends.
findings.quote: Local authorities continue to face significant demand and market pressures, particularly in adults' and children's social care and in the provision of temporary accommodation for homeless households. These challenges are especially pronounced for the council as a London borough.

findings.headline: Ring-fenced schools deficit tripling: DSG account forecast to reach £17.537m by end 2025/26
findings.detail: Ealing's Dedicated Schools Grant account (ring-fenced) held a £5.641m deficit at end 2024/25 and is forecasting £17.537m by Q3 2025/26. This is driven primarily by High Needs Block pressures in special educational needs. Nationally, DSG deficits are forecast to reach £4.6bn by March 2026, up from £3.2bn in March 2025. While the government will write off 90% of the historic deficit in 2026/27, the council still faces ongoing structural SEND funding pressure.
findings.matters: The rapid growth of the DSG deficit signals the current SEND funding model is unsustainable, constraining future flexibility in education spending and indicating a structural problem in meeting statutory special needs duties.
findings.figures: £5.641m DSG deficit end 2024/25; £17.537m forecast Q3 2025/26; national estimate £3.2bn (March 2025) rising to £4.6bn (March 2026)
findings.quote: At the end of 2024/25 the council held a net deficit balance of £5.641m on its DSG account. At the end of Quarter 3 of 2025/26, the council is forecasting a net deficit of £17.537m for the year

findings.headline: Budget path unsustainable: £7.893m deficit forecast by 2029/30 with no mitigation plan
findings.detail: The 2026/27 budget is balanced, but projected budgets show a cumulative deficit of £7.893m by 2029/30. The council explicitly acknowledges this requires 'additional funding and reduced service costs, and/ or additional income to achieve a sustainable budget in the medium-term through to 2030.' No mitigation strategy or solution has yet been identified for this structural imbalance, creating a medium-term refinancing risk.
findings.matters: A lender assessing refinancing risk in 3-4 years needs to understand the council faces difficult decisions on funding or service levels, and current trends are unsustainable without intervention.
findings.figures: £7.893m cumulative deficit by 2029/30
findings.quote: The projected budgets for the next three years show a cumulative deficit of £7.893m by 2029/30. This highlights the need for additional funding and reduced service costs, and/ or additional income to achieve a sustainable budget in the medium-term through to 2030.

findings.headline: Asset disposal timing and value is highly volatile and shortfalls must be met from increased borrowing
findings.detail: Capital receipts from asset sales are identified as the most unpredictable element of capital funding. If disposals underperform against forecast, the council must increase borrowing to cover the gap, up to the agreed Authorised Borrowing Limit. Given the council's stated reluctance to borrow, receipt shortfalls could force difficult trade-offs.
findings.matters: Asset sales volatility creates cash flow and funding risk. A poorly performing property market or delays in disposals would force additional borrowing, directly conflicting with the stated policy of minimising new debt.
findings.figures: Capital receipts planned: £24.059m (General Fund) and £119.657m (HRA) over 2025/26-2030/31
findings.quote: The timing and value of asset sales is the most volatile element of funding. As a result, the Strategic Director, Resources closely monitors progress on asset disposals. Any in-year shortfalls against forecasts will need to be met from increased borrowing, up to the 'Authorised Borrowing Limit' which is agreed annually as part of the Treasury Management Strategy.

findings.headline: Delivery of the council's climate programme is highly dependent on securing competitive government and external grants with no guarantee of success
findings.detail: The council's ability to fund climate investments relies heavily on external funding sources that are competitive and uncertain. Officer time is spent preparing bids to government funding pots. If funding bids fail, the council's climate targets and capital programme commitments may not be deliverable.
findings.matters: Dependence on external grant funding creates delivery risk. A failure to secure expected grants would force either unplanned borrowing (contrary to stated policy) or deferral of committed projects, affecting service and stakeholder confidence.
findings.figures: £14.1m approved capital investment in Greener Ealing Limited includes leasing/vehicles; 150 bike hangars programme continues; Young Adults Centre opened spring 2025
findings.quote: Currently, delivery of the council's climate programme is highly contingent on external funding sources, often originating from government, to fund climate investments, such as schemes relating to corporate and domestic energy efficiency and retrofit. Officer time is required to prepare bids for these funding pots, which are usually competitive, thereby providing no guarantee of success.

findings.headline: The council's medium-term financial strategy shows a balanced budget for 2026/27 but has an unresolved budget gap in future years
findings.detail: While 2026/27 is balanced, the MTFS projects a budget gap beyond that period that will require action. The document does not specify the size of this gap or when it emerges, leaving uncertainty about the severity of future financial pressure.
findings.matters: This signals that the council's financial position will come under pressure in coming years, which affects its ability to service debt, fund capital investment, and maintain services. It may be a precursor to savings plans or service changes.
findings.figures: Capital programme total 2025/26-2030/31: £1,377.78m; budget balanced in 2026/27 only
findings.quote: The council's MTFS shows a balanced budget for 2026/27. However there is a budget gap in future years that will need to be addressed.

findings.headline: Broadway Living Registered Provider's business model is under review with no agreed path forward yet
findings.detail: Following the contractor insolvency and inability to deliver the original plan, BLRP's Managing Director and Board are reviewing options for a viable alternative business plan with external advisers (Campbell Tickell). Proposals are being reviewed for 2025/26 but have not yet been finalised. The impact on the Capital Strategy will be determined once proposals are agreed.
findings.matters: Until BLRP's future model is resolved, there is uncertainty about what capital will be needed, how much council loan funding will be deployed, and what revenue return the council can expect from this investment.
findings.figures: Original plan: 1,471 new homes; current status: 2 schemes complete, 1 at completion, 4 paused
findings.quote: The BLRP Managing Director and Board are now reviewing options for a viable business plan, advised by Campbell Tickell, and proposals are currently being reviewed for the financial year 2025/26. Once those proposals are considered, the impact on the Capital Strategy and Programme will be considered.

findings.headline: From 2026/27, new capital schemes will not be funded from borrowing because the council has high historic debt
findings.detail: The council has explicitly adopted a constraint on its capital programme to avoid further borrowing. This reflects a recognition that existing debt levels are limiting. Any new capital investment will need to come from external grants, capital receipts, or revenue contributions rather than prudential borrowing.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know the council's current debt capacity and constraints. An explicit policy against new borrowing signals fiscal stress and limits the council's future investment flexibility.
findings.figures: £1,456.205m capital programme over 2025/26 to 2030/31; council's MTFS shows a balanced budget for 2026/27 but a budget gap in future years
findings.quote: capital schemes will not be undertaken unless they can be funded from sources other than borrowing, as the council has a high level of historic debt

findings.paper_title: 4.3. Appendix 3 LBE Pension Fund_Forvis Mazars ACR 2024-25
findings.headline: Fund does not perform full user access reviews; only approver-level access reviewed, creating risk of unauthorized journal posting
findings.detail: The audit identified a control deficiency: the fund does not perform a full user access review covering all staff. Only those with approver access were reviewed for appropriateness of system access to Agresso BWO. This gap creates potential for fraudulent journals to be posted. Management is implementing full role reviews as part of Business World migration scheduled for August 2026.
findings.matters: User access controls are fundamental to preventing unauthorized or fraudulent transactions in financial systems; gaps in access reviews indicate control environment weakness affecting the council's financial controls
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: The Fund does not perform a full user access review where appropriateness of access for application user base is considered. We noted that a user access review was not carried out for all staff but only those with approver access.

findings.paper_title: 4.3. Appendix 3 LBE Pension Fund_Forvis Mazars ACR 2024-25
findings.headline: Fund previously misclassified a major investment (Federated Hermes) by over £35 million between fair value hierarchy levels, now corrected
findings.detail: In prior years 2022/23 and 2023/24, the Federated Hermes investment was incorrectly classified as level 2 when it should have been level 3, requiring corrections of £35.6 million and £33 million respectively. This significant deficiency has been resolved after management performed a thorough review of all investment classifications.
findings.matters: Shows the fund has had recurring investment classification governance issues; while now fixed, indicates historical weakness in valuation controls that affect the pension liability measurement
findings.figures: £35,625k correction (2022/23), £32,968k correction (2023/24)
findings.quote: Classification of investments within the fair value hierarchy. We noted that 'Federated Hermes' investment asset was classified as level 2 in both 2022/23 and 2023/24 but should have been level 3. This resulted in a classification adjustment of £35,625k in 2022/23 and £32,968k in 2023/24

findings.headline: Economic headwinds: UK contraction, services output down, employment rates falling, yet council is locked into capital spending plan
findings.detail: The economic background section (paras 68–72) documents UK GDP contraction, services sector output decline of 0.3%, construction down 0.6%, employment rate down 0.3 percentage points to 74.9%, and unemployment rising to 5.1%. The council cannot flex its £535m capital programme despite these macro headwinds without breach of prudential limits.
findings.matters: A weaker economy typically reduces council tax collection, increases demand for welfare services, and erodes business rate bases. The council's fixed capital commitments and rising debt service reduce its ability to pivot if revenues decline.
findings.figures: UK services output: -0.3% (September); construction: -0.6%; trade deficit widened to £4.82bn; employment rate: 74.9% (down 0.3pp); unemployment: 5.1% (up 0.4pp)
findings.quote: The UK economy contracted by 0.1% in October, following a similar decline in September and missing expectations for a 0.1% expansion, marking the fourth consecutive month without growth. Services output declined 0.3% after a 0.2% gain in September, and construction fell 0.6% from a 0.2% rise.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement growing 51% from £1,115m (2025/26) to £1,691m (2028/29)
findings.detail: The council's underlying borrowing need (the CFR, which excludes temporary cash management) will grow by £576m over four years. This is a substantial structural increase in the council's debt burden, driven by capital commitments that are not being offset by asset sales or other financing.
findings.matters: This growth trajectory indicates the council is making significant new capital commitments that will require debt servicing for decades. A lender needs to assess whether the council's revenue base can support this level of indebtedness sustainably, especially with HRA ratios already elevated.

findings.headline: HRA borrowing strategy deferred — council waiting for interest rate falls before raising new HRA debt
findings.detail: The council is NOT currently borrowing for HRA capital needs. Instead, it is using HRA cash balances and short-term General Fund loans. The strategy (para 63) is to 'consider undertaking HRA borrowing' only when interest rates fall from current levels. This creates timing risk: if rates do not fall, HRA financing becomes constrained.
findings.matters: A lender should track whether this deferral is sustainable. If HRA capital programmes proceed as planned but long-term rates remain sticky, the council faces either delayed capital delivery or forced acceptance of higher rates than it would prefer. Current HRA debt-to-revenue ratios already show strain.
findings.figures: Current interest rate forecast: 5yr PWLB at 4.60% (Mar-26) declining to 4.10% (June-27 onwards)
findings.quote: Currently the interest rates are not favourable for new borrowings and interest rates are expected to fall in the coming years, at which point the council will consider undertaking HRA borrowing. In the meantime, it will utilise cash balances and, if necessary, borrow in the short term from the GF.

findings.headline: General Fund overborrowed by £160–544m due to 2021/22 low-rate borrowing that capital programme has not yet consumed
findings.detail: The council borrowed heavily in 2021/22 when PWLB rates were low (strategy outlined in para 73). This created an overborrowed position: actual external debt now exceeds the Capital Financing Requirement, with under-borrowing of £544m forecast for 2026/27 (Table 2B). The council is paying interest on cash it has not yet spent, locked into rates that are now above long-term forecasts.
findings.matters: This represents a locked-in cost: the council has paid for the privilege of borrowing early and is now holding cash earning low rates while paying higher debt rates. It signals a prior treasury misjudgement and constrains future borrowing flexibility if capital programmes slip.
findings.figures: Overborrowing: General Fund positioned with £160.5m under-borrowing at 2024/25, forecast to reach £544.3m by 2026/27. External debt £838.4m vs CFR £1,382.7m (2026/27).
findings.quote: the council was maintaining an under-borrowed position up until 2021/22 when advantageous borrowing rates has led to the council taking out some borrowing early. This means that the capital borrowing need, the CFR, is now funded in advance.

findings.headline: Investment balances collapsing from £527m to £175m over four years — cash reserves draining
findings.detail: The council's treasury investment portfolio is forecast to decline 67% from £527m at 2024/25 outturn to £175m by 2028/29. This reflects application of capital receipts and reserves to fund capital expenditure rather than new resource inflows. The council will have materially less liquidity headroom.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's cash reserves position and ability to absorb shocks. Declining reserves combined with rising debt indicates reduced financial flexibility. If capital schemes slip or income shortfalls occur, the council has less buffer.
findings.quote: Expected Investments 527 431 325 250 175

findings.headline: HRA debt-to-revenue ratio deteriorating sharply from 3.2:1 to 4.6:1 over four years
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account debt is growing faster than rental income. The ratio of HRA debt to annual revenues rises from 3.20:1 in 2024/25 to 4.57:1 in 2026/27 and stays at 4.63:1 by 2028/29. Debt per dwelling rises from £0.025m to £0.040m. This suggests HRA is becoming increasingly leveraged to support housing development.
findings.matters: Deteriorating HRA affordability ratios indicate the council is stretching its housing business model. A lender would question sustainability if rental income growth cannot keep pace with debt growth, especially if interest rates remain higher than forecast or if rental income stalls.

findings.headline: Borrowing for housing company (BLRP) will consume 86% of all new council borrowing by 2028/29
findings.detail: Loans to Broadway Living Registered Provider for housing development represent £57.6m of 2026/27 borrowing (16.7% of total financing need), but explode to £316.2m in 2028/29 (86.2% of total financing need). This is policy/non-treasury lending with different risk profile and repayment tied to housing project completion, not standard revenue flows.
findings.matters: A lender needs to assess whether concentration of nearly £316m (by 2028/29) in a single housing vehicle's debt creates material credit risk, especially if the development encounters cost overruns or market delays. MRP repayment is holiday-funded until asset completion.
findings.figures: 2026/27 BLRP borrowing: £57.647m (16.68% of total need); 2028/29: £316.241m (86.21% of total need)
findings.quote: Borrowing for non-financial investments 4.012 0.000 57.647 0.000 316.241 / Percentage of total external debt % 0% 0% 7% 0% 33%

findings.headline: Capital programme heavily front-loaded to 2026/27 with £535.6m spend, then collapses to £116.8m in 2027/28, then surges to £408.2m in 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's capital expenditure plans show extreme volatility: £535.6m in 2026/27, dropping by 78% to £116.8m in 2027/28, then rising 249% to £408.2m in 2028/29. This lumpy profile creates refinancing and cash-flow timing risks. The 2026/27 spike is driven by a single capital scheme (likely housing).
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether the council can service financing for a heavily front-loaded capital programme that then requires restart of major spending two years later. Refinancing risk concentrates in 2028/29.
findings.quote: Add : Capital Additions/ Repurpose/Decommissioning /Re-profiling of Mainstream Funding 0.000 0.000 24.035 23.130 18.730 / Total Capital Programme including proposed Growth 176.673 271.992 535.601 116.780 408.204

findings.headline: HRA borrowing delayed indefinitely while interest rates remain unfavourable; immediate funding gap being met from General Fund
findings.detail: The council identifies a HRA borrowing need based on liability benchmarking but is deferring new HRA borrowing because 'interest rates are not favourable for new borrowings and interest rates are expected to fall in the coming years'. In the interim, the HRA will use cash balances and may borrow in the short term from the General Fund. This creates uncertainty about timing of HRA borrowing and introduces General Fund/HRA cross-subsidisation.
findings.matters: Delaying HRA borrowing creates refinancing risk if rates do not fall as expected. Using General Fund cash to cover HRA deficits reduces headroom in the General Fund and creates intergenerational fairness issues. Lenders need clarity on whether the council can afford to let interest rates drive major borrowing decisions.
findings.figures: HRA borrowing need exists but deferred pending rate improvement; interim funding from cash balances or General Fund
findings.quote: Currently the interest rates are not favourable for new borrowings and interest rates are expected to fall in the coming years, at which point the council will consider undertaking HRA borrowing. In the meantime, it will utilise cash balances and, if necessary, borrow in the short term from the GF.

findings.headline: Investment balances declining sharply, reducing financial flexibility over the strategy period
findings.detail: The council's available cash balances are forecast to fall from £527m in 2024/25 to £175m by 2028/29, a 67% reduction. The steepest falls occur in 2025/26 (£431m) and 2026/27 (£325m), coinciding with the capital programme acceleration. This reduces the council's liquidity buffer and increases reliance on borrowing.
findings.matters: Declining cash balances reduce the council's capacity to absorb unexpected costs, delays to income, or service pressures. Low balances also mean less investment income to offset borrowing costs, and the council may be forced into higher-cost short-term borrowing if a timing mismatch occurs.

findings.headline: Housing revenue account debt metrics are deteriorating and approaching levels that may constrain borrowing capacity
findings.detail: The HRA debt-to-revenue ratio is rising from 3.20:1 in 2024/25 to 4.39:1 in 2025/26 and stabilising at 4.57:1–4.63:1 through 2028/29. Debt per dwelling is also rising from £0.025m to £0.047m. These metrics show the HRA is becoming increasingly leveraged, particularly as new borrowing is expected.
findings.matters: High debt-to-revenue ratios constrain future borrowing capacity and indicate rising debt service burden on HRA revenues. At 4.63:1, the ratio is above many comparable councils and leaves limited headroom for service pressures or income volatility.

findings.headline: Capital programme nearly doubles in 2026/27 with major concentration in a single housing investment in later years
findings.detail: The capital programme jumps from £272m in 2025/26 to £536m in 2026/27 (including growth), then drops to £117m in 2027/28, then spikes to £408m in 2028/29. The Council's policy loan to Broadway Living RP grows from £0m in 2025/26 to £57.6m in 2026/27 and then £316m in 2028/29, eventually representing 33% of total external debt and 86% of the financing need in that year alone.
findings.matters: Lumpy capital spending creates refinancing and execution risk. The concentration of the housing loan to a single entity (Broadway Living RP) represents a material policy investment with timing and completion risk. Lenders need to understand execution capability for this scale and timing of delivery.
findings.figures: 2026/27 capital: £535.6m; 2027/28: £116.8m; 2028/29: £408.2m; BLRP loan 2028/29: £316.241m (33% of total debt; 86.21% of that year's financing need)

findings.headline: Council remains overborrowed after capital programme delays pushed back project delivery
findings.detail: Ealing borrowed early at advantageous rates in 2021/22 to fund a capital programme, but that programme has experienced delays due to COVID and wider economic conditions. The council is now in an overborrowed position (paying interest on borrowed funds not yet deployed) while waiting for projects to move forward. The overborrowing is expected to reduce over the next couple of years as the capital programme executes.
findings.matters: Timing mismatch between debt service costs and asset delivery creates a drag on revenues until projects are operationalised. It also indicates capital delivery risk if projects continue to slip.
findings.figures: General Fund showing overborrowed position relative to CFR; council expects position to reduce over the next couple of years
findings.quote: the council took advantage of low interest rates borrowings in 2021/22 to fund its planned capital programme. That capital programme has experienced delays due to the impact of covid and the wider economic position, however, the overborrowing position is expected to reduce over the next couple of years.

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee review and report to Council final draft to AC
findings.headline: Risk management strategy last formally approved February 2022, unchanged for over 3.5 years.
findings.detail: The Audit Committee receives regular risk reports and reviews the strategy, but the strategy itself was last formally approved in February 2022. No update or approval of a refreshed strategy is mentioned in this 2025/26 review despite the extended period.
findings.matters: A static risk strategy over 3.5 years is unlikely to reflect changes in council operations, strategic priorities, or emerging risks. Lenders assess governance quality partly through the currency of risk frameworks.
findings.figures: February 2022
findings.quote: A risk report is received at each meeting. This includes a regular review of the strategy (last approved February 2022).

findings.paper_title: Audit Committee review and report to Council final draft to AC
findings.headline: External auditor issued a disclaimed opinion in 2024/25, removing audit assurance on financial statements.
findings.detail: The paper states the external auditor provided a disclaimed opinion during 2024/25. A disclaimed opinion means the auditor could not form an opinion on whether the financial statements are true and fair—the most serious audit outcome. The paper attributes this to national audit backlog delays, though notes the backlog has been 'largely addressed.'
findings.matters: A disclaimed audit opinion eliminates external assurance on financial statement accuracy. This removes a primary control that lenders rely on to verify reported financial position, even if the underlying cause is temporary.
findings.quote: During 2024/25 the audit backlog was largely addressed, although the external auditor provided a disclaimed opinion in line with the national delays and government solution to address audit backlogs.

news_drafts.headline: Business rates collection 2.42% behind target, and declining 2.41% year-on-year
news_drafts.lead: Year-on-year business rates collection decline, beyond government billing delays, signals underlying income risk affecting cash flow and medium-term revenue.

news_drafts.headline: £51.3m of capital schemes decommissioned including 57 Greenford Rd housing block (£32.8m) cancelled
news_drafts.lead: Capital cancellations of this scale reduce investment capacity; loss of £32.8m housing investment matters given the paper's identification of temporary accommodation cost pressures.

news_drafts.headline: DSG deficit forecast to grow to £34.6m by year-end, driven by rising EHCP placement demand
news_drafts.lead: DSG deficit is a balance sheet liability even if ring-fenced; structural EHCP demand growth represents ongoing recurring pressure that affects financial ratios.
